column4: The root of the section's root ج ن ن appears in the night that covers Abraham; seeing the star and then its setting makes darkness a ground for discernment, not mere concealment.
This verse says God darkened the night and brought out its morning brightness, staging the cover and its opening as two successive acts.
The section's root ف ج ر names dawn's splitting; here God is فَالِقُ الْإِصْبَاحِ, the one who cleaves morning from night.
The white thread separates from the black at مِنَ الْفَجْرِ: dawn appears first as a fine boundary, just as the section describes.
The night of decree lasts until مَطْلَعِ الْفَجْرِ, making dawn the precise edge where the covered night ends.
The oath holds night as it darkens or withdraws; 81:18 completes the transition with morning breathing, another night-to-dawn pairing.
Morning breathes in تَنَفَّسَ; this joins the section's opening dawn to its final نَفْس through the root ن ف س, while 81:17 supplies the night before it.
Night turns its back in أَدْبَرَ; the next oath names the clearing morning, matching the section's moving cover and its opening.
Morning brightens in أَسْفَرَ, completing 74:33's departing night and giving a second formulation of the section's dawn.
Night and day are made to cover and pursue one another swiftly, presenting the same layered, moving boundary that the section gives to the night and dawn.
The verse portrays night and day coiling over one another, a repeated wrapping and unwrapping that enlarges the section's single opening into a cycle.
The night is a sign when God strips the day from it in نَسْلَخُ; this reverses the section's dawn splitting into night, while preserving the image of light withdrawn from darkness.
The night is called a garment, لِبَاسًا, directly naming the covering that the section's dawn tears open.
Night again is made a garment, while sleep is rest and day is renewed activity; it develops the section's cover-and-opening scene as a human rhythm.
The oath names night as it covers it in يَغْشَىٰهَا, giving a direct counterpart to the section's night spread over everything.
Day displays it in جَلَّىٰهَا; 91:4 follows with night covering it, completing the same alternating visibility that the section describes.
Night is sworn by as it envelops in يَغْشَىٰ, the full-cover state against which the section's torn opening of dawn is visible.
Day is sworn by as it appears in تَجَلَّىٰ; it completes 92:1's enveloping night with the visible side of the same transition.
The night sign is made dark and the day sign gives sight; this states the concealment and disclosure that the section makes into a slit of dawn.
When Moses strikes the rock, water bursts from it in انفَجَرَتْ; the same root's force of opening out adds a concrete outflow to the section's dawn-splitting image.
The earth's springs burst forth in فَجَّرْنَا after the flood, carrying the section's root ف ج ر from dawn's opening into water breaking out of the ground.
The requested garden of palms and vines includes streams bursting through it in تُفَجِّرَ; the root joins an opening flow to the garden that closes the section.
Between the two gardens a stream is made to burst in فَجَّرْنَا, uniting the section's root for dawn's rupture with its final covered garden.
The criminals call حِجْرًا مَحْجُورًا when they see the angels; the exact root named for reason-as-restraint appears here as an impassable boundary at judgment.
The earth and mountains are pounded in فَدُكَّتَا دَكَّةً وَاحِدَةً, a direct parallel to 89:21's repeated pounding of the earth.
The graves are overturned in بُعْثِرَتْ الْقُبُورُ; the earth's burial-cover is opened, matching the section's cenen/grave sense and its pounded earth.
The earth casts out what is inside it in أَلْقَتْ مَا فِيهَا, making the hidden contents of the ground visible as the section's grave-cover and crushed-earth images imply.
The earth brings out its burdens in أَخْرَجَتِ الْأَرْضُ أَثْقَالَهَا, a direct scene of what was covered below being exposed.
What is in the graves is scattered in بُعْثِرَ مَا فِي الْقُبُورِ; 100:10 then names what is within the chests, extending judgment's disclosure beyond the earth-cover.
People hurry from the graves toward their Lord, مِنَ الْأَجْدَاثِ إِلَىٰ رَبِّهِمْ; the grave's cover gives way to the soul's final approach to the Lord.
The garden is framed by vines and palms surrounding it, حَفَفْنَاهُمَا بِنَخْلٍ; this gives a Quranic scene for the section's garden as foliage that hides the earth.
The promised comfort is something hidden from people today, أُخْفِيَ لَهُم; this states directly the concealed reward that the section hears inside جَنَّتِي.
At death the angels greet the good and tell them to enter the Garden; this closely joins the section's calm soul, peaceful return, and final command to enter.
The Garden's gates open and its keepers welcome those entering; the verse supplies the threshold and welcome implicit in the section's repeated command to enter.
The righteous enter Eden with their families, and angels greet them at its gates; this develops the section's entry among God's servants and into the Garden.
The invitation is explicit: enter it in peace; the destination and secure entry echo the section's final call to enter the Garden.
The verse joins gardens of Eden with God being pleased with the people and their being pleased with Him, closely paralleling the section's soul that is pleased and pleasing as it enters the Garden.
The verse names the time before the dawn prayer as a household privacy period; it treats الفجر as a precise boundary in daily life, like the section's narrow dawn line.
The dawn recitation is singled out as witnessed, locating الفجر at the transition from night into a distinct morning interval, as in the section's threshold image.
Moses' appointed time is counted as thirty nights completed by ten; this gives the section's ten nights a Quranic counterpart as successive nights rather than one dark span.
The oath introduces the night-comer, and 86:3 identifies it as a piercing star; together they make a point of light puncture the darkness like the section's first slit in the night-cover.
The star is called piercing, النَّجْمُ الثَّاقِبُ; 86:1 places it in the night, a specific image of light entering darkness at a point.
The refuge prayer names darkness when it settles; 113:1's al-falaq supplies the possible dawn-opening counterpart to the section's night and dawn.
The root ف ل ق is explicitly linked by the section to dawn's splitting, but al-falaq can also mean creation generally; on the dawn reading, the refuge begins by naming the Lord of the opening.

The oath names night and what it gathers; the exact force of وَمَا وَسَقَ is uncertain, but a gathering night plausibly develops the section's image of darkness drawing a cover over what lies beneath.
This oath gives night in its stillness, while the section's night is pictured moving on; it preserves a distinct night-state beside the traveling cover.
Night and day enter into one another here, a specific formulation of the threshold crossing that the section stages as a cover shifting away.
The soul is shaped before 91:8 names its fujur and taqwa; this starts the moral choice that the section's inner restraint and tranquil soul bring into view.
The one who purifies the soul succeeds; 91:8 defines the competing moral qualities, and this outcome parallels the section's call to the tranquil soul.
The one who buries or corrupts the soul fails, completing 91:8's fujur/taqwa division as a moral counterpart to the section's two kinds of rupture.
The wrongdoers' deeds leave rust over their hearts, رَانَ عَلَىٰ قُلُوبِهِمْ; this is a counter-image to the section's moral “tearing” of a cover, showing wrongdoing can also thicken concealment.
Lot is told to travel by night with his family using the same س ر ي root as the section's moving night; here people move under night rather than night itself moving.
Lot is again told to travel during part of the night with س ر ي; the repeated command gives the section's night-journey root a concrete human scene.
Moses is commanded to travel at night with his people using the same root; the passage makes night a route crossed by travelers, alongside the section's personified night journey.
Moses receives the same night-travel command from the س ر ي root, extending the section's moving-night word into the Exodus scene.
The command to travel by night repeats the section's س ر ي root; its context makes night the passage through which a people depart.
The night journey begins with أَسْرَىٰ بِعَبْدِهِ لَيْلًا; the same root depicts a human journey through night, alongside the section's night moving on.
The one who restrains the self from desire, نَهَى النَّفْسَ عَنِ الْهَوَىٰ, embodies the inner wall that the section says reason places against wrongdoing.
That person's refuge is the Garden; 79:40 supplies the restraint that leads to a destination echoing the section's final Garden-entry.
The verse calls God's ordinances boundaries and forbids crossing them; it states in law the containing function that the section gives the mind's inner wall.
The command not to transgress the balance gives a specific moral limit, echoing the restraint that the section hears in ḥijr.
Success is tied to being protected from the self's avarice; this is a concrete inward restraint comparable to the section's reason-as-barrier.
The proud are barred from the Garden, with a gate that will not open and entry made impossible; this joins the section's wall-like restraint to its final Garden threshold.
Hypocrites take their oaths as a shield, جُنَّةً, using the same covering root named for night and Garden; here concealment protects falsehood rather than opening into light.
Their oaths are again a shield, جُنَّةً, but now explicitly conceal their rejection; it gives the section's cover-root a morally opposite use.
Satan tempts the pair so that what was concealed of their nakedness becomes apparent; this contrasts exposure caused by disobedience with dawn's clear opening.
In the Garden, shade lies close over its people and its fruits hang low; this gives a concrete leafy shelter for the section's hidden, tree-covered Garden image.
A barrier stands before the dead until resurrection, بَرْزَخٌ; 23:99 supplies the plea to return, contrasting that blocked passage with the section's welcomed return to God.
At death a person pleads, رَبِّ ارْجِعُونِ, to be sent back; this reverses the section's serene soul being told to return to its Lord.
The hearts become tranquil, تَطْمَئِنُّ الْقُلُوبُ, echoing the section's نَفْسُ الْمُطْمَئِنَّةُ and giving a distinct Quranic setting for inward rest.
Abraham asks for a sign of revival so that his heart may be reassured; in the section's resurrection-to-return arc, this gives reassurance a concrete relation to seeing what follows death.
The barrier is made level in دَكَّاءَ when God's promise arrives; this joins the section's pounding root to a boundary finally flattened.
The mountain is made level in دَكًّا at the theophany; the same root as the section's crushed earth appears in a scene of divine force breaking a solid surface.
God causes the human to die and be placed in a grave, فَأَقْبَرَهُ; this makes the section's grave-as-cover sense concrete at the passage from life to burial.
What is in the chests is brought out; 100:9 names the opened graves, and this verse extends the disclosure from earth's cover to hidden inward contents.
Those raised from their resting place ask who awakened them; 36:51 supplies the graves they have just left, completing the section's movement from grave-cover toward the Lord.
The same fujur root is placed opposite taqwa in the soul; the moral rupture is the dark counter-side to the section's dawn-splitting image.
The person wants to keep sinning ahead, لِيَفْجُرَ أَمَامَهُ; the root's moral branch makes a deliberate breach where dawn's rupture brings light.
The fujjar end in the Fire; the shared root marks moral rupture as the opposite outcome to the section's opening dawn and its final garden.
The record of the fujjar is in Sijjīn; this directly names the root's moral branch as a destination opposite to the Garden at the section's end.
The wicked at judgment are called al-fajarah; the dawn-root's moral branch describes a human outcome opposite to the light opening in the section.
Adam and his spouse are expelled from the Garden, the inverse of the section's last invitation to enter God's Garden.
Satan's expulsion of Adam's parents from the Garden includes stripping their clothes; it reverses the section's final entry and makes concealment fail through disobedience.
After eating, the pair's nakedness appears and they cover themselves with Garden leaves; wrongdoing brings a shameful exposure, unlike dawn's revealing light.
Those rejecting their Lord are told to enter Hell's gates; 39:73 follows with the Garden's gates opening, framing the section's final invitation as the blessed side of a divided destination.
